metadata.title: On the unicity of types for toral supercuspidal representations

extraction_notes.note: The unnumbered introduction theorem restates Theorem 7.3 but also adds the 'only if' direction for strong unicity, which comes from Lemma 8.1. nodes.name: Bernstein block
nodes.statement: In \cite{Bernstein1984}, J.~Bernstein gives a decomposition of the category of smooth representations of $G$ into indecomposable full subcategories, called \emph{blocks}, that are indexed by the inertial support of the irreducible representations they contain.
nodes.statement_short: Bernstein decomposes smooth representations of $G$ into blocks indexed by inertial support.

nodes.name: Type (Bushnell-Kutzko type)
nodes.statement: Given an irreducible supercuspidal representation $\pi$ of $G$, a \emph{type} for $\pi$ is a pair $(K, \lambda)$ consisting of an irreducible representation $\lambda$ of a compact open subgroup $K$ of $G$ such that $\mathrm{Ind}_K^G \lambda$ is a projective generator of the block containing $\pi$.
nodes.genus: a pair $(K, \lambda)$ consisting of an irreducible representation $\lambda$ of a compact open subgroup $K$ of $G$
differentia: $\mathrm{Ind}_K^G \lambda$ is a projective generator of the block containing $\pi$
nodes.statement_short: A type for $\pi$ is $(K,\lambda)$ with $\mathrm{Ind}_K^G\lambda$ a projective generator of $\pi$'s Bernstein block.

nodes.name: Representation containing a type
nodes.statement: In this case, $\lambda$ occurs as a subrepresentation of $\pi|_K$ and we say $\pi$ \emph{contains} the type $(K,\lambda)$.

nodes.name: Existence of types for essentially tame supercuspidals (Adler, Yu, Kim)
nodes.statement: In particular, the work of J.~Adler \cite{Adler1998}, generalized by J.K.~Yu \cite{Yu2001}, shows that every essentially tame supercuspidal representation contains a type; the work of J.-L.~Kim \cite{Kim2007} assures us that if the residual characteristic $p$ is sufficiently large, then all supercuspidal representations of $G$ are of this form.
assumptions: if the residual characteristic $p$ is sufficiently large
conclusions: every essentially tame supercuspidal representation contains a type
all supercuspidal representations of $G$ are of this form
nodes.statement_short: Every essentially tame supercuspidal contains a type, and for large $p$ all supercuspidals are essentially tame.

nodes.name: Conjugates and enlargements of types are types
nodes.statement: Given a supercuspidal representation $\pi$ of $G$ containing a type $(K,\lambda)$, it is simple to produce additional types: any $G$-conjugate of $(K,\lambda)$ is a type, as is any pair $(K', \tau)$ where $K'$ is a compact open subgroup of $G$ containing $K$ and $\tau$ is an irreducible representation of $K'$ that contains $\lambda$ upon restriction to $K$.
assumptions: Given a supercuspidal representation $\pi$ of $G$ containing a type $(K,\lambda)$
conclusions: any $G$-conjugate of $(K,\lambda)$ is a type
nodes.statement_short: $G$-conjugates of a type, and irreducible reps of larger compact open subgroups containing it, are again types.

nodes.name: Unicity of types
nodes.statement: A natural question to ask is whether $\pi$ can contain any additional types, specifically on \emph{maximal} compact open subgroups, that are not related to $(K,\lambda)$ in this way. It is expected that this should never happen, and the conjecture that this is the case is known as the \emph{unicity of types}.
conclusions: It is expected that this should never happen
nodes.statement_short: Every type of $\pi$ on a maximal compact open subgroup arises by conjugating or enlarging a given type.

nodes.name: Known cases of the unicity conjecture
nodes.statement: The unicity conjecture is a theorem for $G=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)$ \cite{Paskunas2005}, $G=\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ \cite{Latham2016}, for essentially tame representations of $G=\mathrm{SL}_n(F)$ \cite{Latham2018}, and for depth-zero supercuspidal representations of any connected reductive $p$-adic group $G$ \cite{Latham2017}.
conclusions: The unicity conjecture is a theorem for $G=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)$ \cite{Paskunas2005}, $G=\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ \cite{Latham2016}
nodes.statement_short: Unicity of types holds for $\mathrm{GL}_n$, $\mathrm{SL}_2$, essentially tame reps of $\mathrm{SL}_n$ and depth-zero supercuspidals.

nodes.name: Strong unicity property
nodes.statement: In each of these cases, it was seen that a stronger property holds, namely, that if $K\subset G$ is any maximal compact open subgroup, then there exists, up to $G$-conjugacy, at most one type defined on $K$ for each supercuspidal representation $\pi$ of $G$. We will refer to this as the \emph{strong unicity property}.
nodes.statement_short: Strong unicity: on each maximal compact open subgroup $K$ there is at most one type for $\pi$ up to $G$-conjugacy.

nodes.name: Toral supercuspidal representation
nodes.statement: We restrict our attention here to those sequences for which the smallest twisted Levi subgroup is an anisotropic (also called elliptic) maximal torus of $G$. For the purposes of this paper we call these \emph{toral} supercuspidal representations, though we caution the reader that some authors reserve ``toral'' to mean the more restrictive case that the twisted Levi sequence has length $d=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Toral supercuspidals: essentially tame ones whose smallest twisted Levi subgroup is an anisotropic maximal torus.

nodes.name: Reformulation of the unicity conjecture
nodes.statement: The conjecture of unicity of types therefore amounts to the statement that, up to $G$-conjugacy, all types for $\pi$ on a maximal compact open subgroup arise in this way.
nodes.statement_short: Unicity: up to $G$-conjugacy every type on a maximal compact is induced from $(\mathsf{K},\kappa)$.

nodes.name: Reformulation of strong unicity
nodes.statement: Strong unicity is the statement that furthermore any two types for $\pi$ on $G_y$ are conjugate by an element of $N_G(G_y)$; this is equivalent to the statement that $(\mathsf{K},\kappa)$ is not contained two distinct but conjugate maximal compact open subgroups.
nodes.statement_short: Strong unicity means types on $G_y$ are $N_G(G_y)$-conjugate, i.e. $(\mathsf{K},\kappa)$ lies in no two distinct conjugate maximal compacts.

nodes.name: Branching rules for restriction to maximal compact subgroups
nodes.statement: The restriction of $\pi$ to a maximal compact open subgroup $G_y$ decomposes as an infinite direct sum of irreducible representations of $G_y$. Describing these branching rules is a difficult open problem of interest in its own right.
nodes.statement_short: Describe the decomposition of $\pi|_{G_y}$ into irreducibles (branching rules).

nodes.name: Justification: block generated by pi
nodes.statement: Here, it suffices to note that with $G$ as above, the Bernstein block corresponding to $\pi$ is generated by $\pi$.
nodes.statement_short: The Bernstein block of $\pi$ is generated by $\pi$ itself.

nodes.name: Types are the components not shared with other representations
nodes.statement: Therefore the types of $\pi$ supported on $G_y$ are exactly those irreducible components of $\pi|_{G_y}$ that do not occur in $\pi'|_{G_y}$ for any other (inequivalent) irreducible representation $\pi'$ of $G$.
conclusions: the types of $\pi$ supported on $G_y$ are exactly those irreducible components of $\pi|_{G_y}$ that do not occur in $\pi'|_{G_y}$ for any other (inequivalent) irreducible representation $\pi'$ of $G$
nodes.statement_short: Types of $\pi$ on $G_y$ are the components of $\pi|_{G_y}$ not occurring in any inequivalent $\pi'|_{G_y}$.

nodes.name: Main theorem (introduction): unicity for toral supercuspidals
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a tame elliptic maximal torus of $G$ and suppose $\pi$ is a supercuspidal representation of $G$ built from a datum containing $T$. If the character $\phi_0$ of $T$ appearing in the datum has depth greater than $2c_T$, then $\pi$ satisfies the unicity conjecture relative to any maximal compact open subgroup of $G$. Moreover, in this case, $\pi$ satisfies the strong unicity property if and only if $\mathcal{B}^T$ consists precisely of the closure of a single facet in $\mathcal{B}(G)$.
assumptions: Let $T$ be a tame elliptic maximal torus of $G$ and suppose $\pi$ is a supercuspidal representation of $G$ built from a datum containing $T$.
If the character $\phi_0$ of $T$ appearing in the datum has depth greater than $2c_T$
conclusions: $\pi$ satisfies the unicity conjecture relative to any maximal compact open subgroup of $G$.
$\pi$ satisfies the strong unicity property if and only if $\mathcal{B}^T$ consists precisely of the closure of a single facet in $\mathcal{B}(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: If depth$(\phi_0)>2c_T$, unicity of types holds; strong unicity holds iff $\mathcal{B}^T$ is the closure of one facet.

nodes.name: Local field F
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a nonarchimedean local field of residual characteristic $p$, with integer ring ${\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}$ and maximal ideal $\mathfrak{p}$.

nodes.name: Normalized valuation
nodes.statement:
We normalize the valuation $
u$ on $F$ so that $
u(F^	imes) =\mathbb{Z}$; if $E$ is an extension field of $F$ then we also denote by $
u$ the unique extension of this valuation to $E$.

nodes.name: Additive character Lambda
nodes.statement: Fix an additive character $\Lambda$ of $F$ that is nontrivial on ${\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}$ but trivial on $\mathfrak{p}$.

nodes.name: Conjugate subgroup and representation
nodes.statement: If $H\subset G$ are groups and $g\in G$, let ${}^gH = \{ghg^{-1}\mid h\in H\}$ and for any representation $\tau$ of $H$ let ${}^g\tau$ denote the corresponding representation of ${}^gH$.

nodes.name: Restriction notation
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ is a representation of $G$ we write $\mathrm{Res}_H\sigma$ for its restriction to $H$.

nodes.name: The group G
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{G}$ be a semisimple simply connected linear algebraic group defined over $F$ and let $G = \mathbf{G}(F)$.

nodes.name: Bruhat-Tits building
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{B}(G)=\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{G},F)$ denote the reduced building of $\mathbf{G}$ over $F$; since $\mathbf{G}$ is semisimple it coincides with the enlarged building.

nodes.name: Point stabilizers are parahoric
nodes.statement: Since $\mathbf{G}$ is simply connected, the stabilizer of a point $x$ in the building, $G_x$, coincides with the parahoric subgroup $G_{x,0}$ associated to the facet containing $x$.
assumptions: Since $\mathbf{G}$ is simply connected
conclusions: the stabilizer of a point $x$ in the building, $G_x$, coincides with the parahoric subgroup $G_{x,0}$ associated to the facet containing $x$

nodes.name: Maximal compact subgroups are vertex stabilizers
nodes.statement: Both hypotheses together imply that the maximal compact open subgroups of $G$ are exactly the maximal parahoric subgroups of $G$, that is, $G_y$ for each vertex $y$ of the building.
conclusions: the maximal compact open subgroups of $G$ are exactly the maximal parahoric subgroups of $G$, that is, $G_y$ for each vertex $y$ of the building

nodes.name: Maximal split torus S
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{S}$ be a maximal $F$-split torus in $\mathbf{G}$ defined over $F$.

nodes.name: Maximal unramified-split torus S'
nodes.statement: Fix a maximal unramified extension $F^{un}$ of $F$, and let $\mathbf{S}'$ be a maximal $F^{un}$-split torus of $\mathbf{G}$ defined over $F$ and containing $\mathbf{S}$.

nodes.name: Torus Z
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{Z}$ be the centralizer of $\mathbf{S}'$ in $\mathbf{G}$, which is a maximal torus of $\mathbf{G}$ defined over $F$.

nodes.name: Root system and apartment
nodes.statement: Denote by $\Phi = \Phi(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{S})$ the root system of $\mathbf{G}$ relative to $\mathbf{S}$ and by ${\mathcal{A}} = {\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{S}, F)$ the apartment of $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{G},F)$ corresponding to $\mathbf{S}$.

nodes.name: Affine roots
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi_\Phi$ be the set of affine roots, corresponding to our choice of valuation $\nu$; these are functions on ${\mathcal{A}}$.

nodes.name: Root subgroup
nodes.statement: Denote the root subgroup of $\mathbf{G}$ corresponding to $\alpha \in \Phi$ by $\mathbf{G}_\alpha$.

nodes.name: Filtration of root subgroups
nodes.statement: For $\alpha \in \Phi$ we set $G_\alpha=\mathbf{G}_{\alpha}(F)$; this group admits a filtration by compact open subgroups $G_\psi$, as $\psi$ runs over the affine roots with gradient $\dot\psi=\alpha$.

nodes.name: F-points S, S', Z
nodes.statement: Let $S=\mathbf{S}(F)$, $S'=\mathbf{S}'(F)$ and $Z=\mathbf{Z}(F)$.

nodes.name: Maximal bounded subgroup Z_b
nodes.statement: Let $Z_{\mathrm{b}}$ be the maximal bounded subgroup of $Z$.

nodes.name: Filtration of a torus
nodes.statement: Recall that any torus $T=\mathbf{T}(F)$ admits a natural filtration by subgroups $T_r$ for $r\geq 0$, and its Lie algebra $\mathfrak{t}$ is filtered by lattices $\mathfrak{t}_r$ for $r\in \mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Filtration of Z
nodes.statement: In particular, $Z$ admits a natural filtration by subgroups $Z_{r}$ for $r\geq 0$, with $Z_0\subseteq Z_{\mathrm{b}}$.

nodes.name: Moy-Prasad filtration subgroups
nodes.statement: For any $x\in {\mathcal{A}}$ and $r\geq 0$, A.~Moy and G.~Prasad \cite{MoyPrasad1994} defined $G_{\alpha,x,r} = \langle G_\psi \mid \psi(x)\geq r, \dot\psi=\alpha \rangle$ and thus filtration subgroups $$ G_{x,r}=\langle Z_{r}, G_{\alpha,x,r} \mid \alpha \in \Phi\rangle $$ of $G_x$.
nodes.statement_short: Moy-Prasad filtration $G_{x,r}$ generated by $Z_r$ and affine root subgroups $G_\psi$ with $\psi(x)\ge r$.

nodes.name: G_{x,r+}
nodes.statement: We set $G_{x,r+} = \cup_{s>r}G_{x,s}$.

nodes.name: Moy-Prasad lattices
nodes.statement: They similarly defined lattices $\mathfrak{g}_{x,r}$ in $\mathfrak{g}=\mathrm{Lie}(G)(F)$ and $\mathfrak{g}^*_{x,r}$ in $\mathfrak{g}^*$, indexed by $r\in \mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Twisted Levi subgroup
nodes.statement: We say that a group $\mathbf{G}'$ (or its set of $F$-points $G' = \mathbf{G}'(F)$) is a \emph{twisted Levi subgroup} of $\mathbf{G}$ if there is an extension $E$ of $F$ such that $\mathbf{G}'$ is an $E$-Levi subgroup of $\mathbf{G}$ defined over $F$.
differentia: there is an extension $E$ of $F$ such that $\mathbf{G}'$ is an $E$-Levi subgroup of $\mathbf{G}$ defined over $F$

nodes.name: Tamely ramified twisted Levi subgroup
nodes.statement: We say $\mathbf{G}'$ is tamely ramified if $\mathbf{G}'$ (and thus $\mathbf{G}$) splits over a tamely ramified extension.

nodes.name: Torus T and splitting field E of G'
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $\mathbf{G}'$ is a (tamely ramified) twisted Levi subgroup of $\mathbf{G}$ and let $\mathbf{T}$ be a maximal torus of $\mathbf{G}'$; let $E$ be a tamely ramified splitting field of $\mathbf{T}$ over $F$.

nodes.name: Lie algebra g' and dual center z'*
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{g}'$ denote the $F$-points of $\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G}')$, and denote by ${\mathfrak{z}'}^*$ the $F$-points of the dual of the center of $\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G}')$.

nodes.name: G-generic element of depth -r
nodes.statement: Let $r>0$. Following \cite[Definition 3.7]{HakimMurnaghan2008}, an element $X^* \in {\mathfrak{z}'}^*_{-r}$ is called \emph{$G$-generic of depth $-r$} if it satisfies the conditions \textbf{GE1} and \textbf{GE2} of \cite[\S8]{Yu2001}.

nodes.name: Yu's Lemma 8.1 (genericity criterion)
nodes.statement: By \cite[Lemma 8.1]{Yu2001}, if $p$ is not a torsion prime for the root datum (in the sense of \cite{Springer1977}) of $(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{T})$, then these conditions reduce to the requirement that $\nu(\langle X^*, H_a\rangle) = -r$, for each $a \in \Phi(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{T})\setminus\Phi(\mathbf{G}',\mathbf{T})$, where $H_a \in \mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G})(E)$ is the coroot associated to $a$.
assumptions: if $p$ is not a torsion prime for the root datum (in the sense of \cite{Springer1977}) of $(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{T})$
conclusions: these conditions reduce to the requirement that $\nu(\langle X^*, H_a\rangle) = -r$, for each $a \in \Phi(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{T})\setminus\Phi(\mathbf{G}',\mathbf{T})$
nodes.statement_short: For $p$ not a torsion prime, genericity means $\nu(\langle X^*,H_a\rangle)=-r$ for all roots $a$ outside $G'$.

nodes.name: Moy-Prasad isomorphism
nodes.statement: Fix also a Moy-Prasad isomorphism \cite[\S 2.6]{HakimMurnaghan2008} $$ e \colon G'_{x,r}/G'_{x,r+} \to \mathfrak{g}'_{x,r}/\mathfrak{g}'_{x,r+}. $$

nodes.name: Character realized by an element
nodes.statement: A character $\phi$ of $G'$ of depth $r$ is said to be \emph{realized by an element $X^* \in {\mathfrak{z}'}^{*}_{-r}$ on $G'_{x,r}$} if for every $Y \in \mathfrak{g}'_{x,r}$, $$ \phi(e(Y+\mathfrak{g}'_{x,r+})) = \Lambda(\langle X^*, Y\rangle). $$
nodes.statement_short: $\phi$ is realized by $X^*$ on $G'_{x,r}$ if $\phi(e(Y))=\Lambda(\langle X^*,Y\rangle)$ for all $Y\in\mathfrak{g}'_{x,r}$.

nodes.name: G-generic character
nodes.statement: By \cite[Definition 3.9]{HakimMurnaghan2008}, $\phi$ is \emph{$G$-generic (relative to $x$) of depth $r>0$} if $\phi$ is trivial on $G'_{x,r+}$, nontrivial on $G'_{x,r}$, and is realized on $G'_{x,r}$ by an element $X^* \in {\mathfrak{z}'}^{*}_{-r}$ that is $G$-generic of depth $-r$.
differentia: is realized on $G'_{x,r}$ by an element $X^* \in {\mathfrak{z}'}^{*}_{-r}$ that is $G$-generic of depth $-r$
nodes.statement_short: $\phi$ is $G$-generic of depth $r$ if it has depth exactly $r$ at $x$ and is realized by a $G$-generic element.

nodes.name: Yu's Lemma 8.3 (intertwining of generic characters)
nodes.statement: A particular consequence of the $G$-genericity of a character $\phi$ of $G'$ is that for any $g\in G$, we have that ${}^g\phi$ and $\phi$ coincide on $G'_{x,r}$ if and only if $g\in G'$ \cite[Lemma 8.3]{Yu2001}.
conclusions: for any $g\in G$, we have that ${}^g\phi$ and $\phi$ coincide on $G'_{x,r}$ if and only if $g\in G'$
nodes.statement_short: For a $G$-generic character $\phi$ of $G'$, ${}^g\phi=\phi$ on $G'_{x,r}$ iff $g\in G'$.

nodes.name: Toral supercuspidal datum
nodes.statement: Following \cite[\S3]{Yu2001} and \cite[\S3.1]{HakimMurnaghan2008}, we define a \emph{positive-depth generic toral supercuspidal datum of length $d$} of $G$ (hereafter: \emph{toral supercuspidal datum}) to be a pair $(\vec{G}, \vec{\phi})$, where \begin{itemize} \item $\vec{G} = (G^0\subsetneq G^1 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq G^d=G)$, for some $d \geq 1$, is a sequence of tamely ramified twisted Levi subgroups, such that in particular $G^0=T$ an anisotropic maximal torus in $G$; \item $\vec{\phi} = (\phi_0, \phi_1, \ldots, \phi_{d-1})$ where $\phi_i$ is a $G^{i+1}$-generic character of $G^i$ of depth $r_i$, and these real numbers satisfy $0<r_0<r_1 < \cdots < r_{d-1}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations
nodes.definiendum: positive-depth generic toral supercuspidal datum of length $d$
nodes.statement_short: A toral datum: a tower of tame twisted Levis from an anisotropic torus $T$ to $G$, with generic characters of increasing depths $r_i$.

nodes.name: Half depths s_i
nodes.statement: For convenience we write $s_i = r_i/2$ for each $i = 0, \ldots, d-1$.

nodes.name: Embedding of buildings of twisted Levi subgroups
nodes.statement: Given a tamely ramified twisted Levi subgroup $\mathbf{G}'$ of $\mathbf{G}$ that is defined over $F$, one may embed $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{G}',F)$ into $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{G},F)$ with canonical image.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations
conclusions: one may embed $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{G}',F)$ into $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{G},F)$ with canonical image

nodes.name: The point x attached to T
nodes.statement: Since $T$ is anisotropic, the image of $\mathcal{B}(T)$ in $\mathcal{B}(G)$ consists of a single point $x$, and it is this point relative to which the characters $\phi_i$ are $G^{i+1}$-generic.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: Subgroups K^i
nodes.statement: Set $\mathsf{K}^0=G^0_x=T$. For each $1\leq i\leq d$ define $$ \mathsf{K}^i:= G^0_{x}G^1_{x,s_0}\cdots G^{i}_{x,s_{i-1}} \subseteq TG_{x,s_0} \subseteq G_x. $$

nodes.name: Properties of J^i relative to K^i
nodes.statement: The groups in these products have large pairwise intersections, so we next define subgroups $\mathsf{J}^i$ and $\mathsf{J}^i_+$ which will have the property that $\mathsf{K}^i\mathsf{J}^{i+1}=\mathsf{K}^{i+1}$ and $\mathsf{K}^i\cap \mathsf{J}^{i+1} = \mathsf{K}^i\cap \mathsf{J}^{i+1}_+ = G^i_{x,r_i}$.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.statement: Let $E$ be a tamely ramified Galois extension of $F$ over which $\mathbf{T}$ splits.

nodes.statement: These subgroups of $\mathbf{G}^{i+1}(E)$ are invariant under $\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$ and we set $\mathsf{J}^{i+1}=\mathsf{J}(E)^{i+1}\cap G^{i+1}$, $\mathsf{J}^{i+1}_+ = \mathsf{J}(E)^{i+1}_+\cap G^{i+1}$.

The first step is to extend the restriction of $\phi_i$ to $G^i_{x,r_i}$ trivially to a character $\hat\phi_i$ of $J^{i+1}_+$ \cite[\S4]{Yu2001}.

nodes.name: Representation phi_i' of K^{i+1}
nodes.statement: Next, when $\mathsf{J}^{i+1}_+=\mathsf{J}^{i+1}$, define a character $\phi_i'$ of $\mathsf{K}^{i+1}$ by \begin{equation} \phi_i'(kj)=\phi_i(k)\hat\phi_i(j), \end{equation} for each $k\in \mathsf{K}^i$, $j\in \mathsf{J}^{i+1}$. On the other hand, when $\mathsf{J}^{i+1}_+ \neq \mathsf{J}^{i+1}$, then instead one uses $\hat\phi_i$ to construct a Heisenberg-Weil representation $\omega$ of $\mathsf{K}^i\ltimes \mathsf{J}^{i+1}$, and then define the representation $\phi_i'$ on $k\in \mathsf{K}^i$, $j\in \mathsf{J}^{i+1}$ by \begin{equation} \phi_i'(kj) = \phi_i(k)\omega(k,j). \end{equation}

nodes.statement: There is a well-defined inflation process extending each $\phi_i'$ trivially across the remaining subgroups to give a representation of $\mathsf{K}$, which we denote $\kappa_i=\inf_{\mathsf{K}^{i+1}}^{\mathsf{K}}\phi_i'$ \cite[\S3.4]{HakimMurnaghan2008}.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: Hakim-Murnaghan Proposition 3.26 (independence of kappa_i)
nodes.statement: Note that this representation $\kappa_i$ is independent of any other characters $\phi_j$, $j\neq i$, in the datum \cite[Proposition 3.26]{HakimMurnaghan2008}.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations
conclusions: this representation $\kappa_i$ is independent of any other characters $\phi_j$, $j\neq i$, in the datum

nodes.name: Yu's Theorem 15.1 (construction of supercuspidal representations)
nodes.statement: Putting these together, we obtain a representation $\kappa(\Psi)= \kappa_{0}\otimes \cdots \otimes \kappa_{d-1}$ of $\mathsf{K}$ such that $\pi (\Psi) = \textrm{c-}\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathsf{K}}^G \kappa(\Psi)$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $G$ of depth $r=r_{d-1}$ \cite[Theorem 15.1]{Yu2001}.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations
conclusions: $\pi (\Psi) = \textrm{c-}\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathsf{K}}^G \kappa(\Psi)$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $G$ of depth $r=r_{d-1}$
nodes.statement_short: $\pi(\Psi)=\textrm{c-Ind}_{\mathsf{K}}^G\kappa(\Psi)$, $\kappa(\Psi)=\otimes\kappa_i$, is irreducible supercuspidal of depth $r_{d-1}$.

nodes.name: (K, kappa(Psi)) is a type
nodes.statement: It then follows that $(\mathsf{K},\kappa(\Psi))$ is a type for $\pi(\Psi)$.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations
conclusions: $(\mathsf{K},\kappa(\Psi))$ is a type for $\pi(\Psi)$

nodes.name: Hakim-Murnaghan equivalence criterion
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ and $\dot\Psi = (\vec{\dot{G}}, \vec{\dot{\phi}})$ be two toral supercuspidal data. Then $\pi(\Psi) \cong \pi(\dot\Psi)$ if and only if there exists some $g\in G$ such that $G^0 = {}^g\dot{G}^0$ and $\mathrm{Res}_{G^0}(\phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})=\mathrm{Res}_{G^0}{}^g(\dot{\phi}_0 \dot{\phi}_1 \cdots \dot{\phi}_{d-1})$. In this case, $G^i={}^g\dot{G}^i$ for all $i\geq 0$.
assumptions: Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ and $\dot\Psi = (\vec{\dot{G}}, \vec{\dot{\phi}})$ be two toral supercuspidal data.
conclusions: $\pi(\Psi) \cong \pi(\dot\Psi)$ if and only if there exists some $g\in G$ such that $G^0 = {}^g\dot{G}^0$ and $\mathrm{Res}_{G^0}(\phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})=\mathrm{Res}_{G^0}{}^g(\dot{\phi}_0 \dot{\phi}_1 \cdots \dot{\phi}_{d-1})$.
In this case, $G^i={}^g\dot{G}^i$ for all $i\geq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi(\Psi)\cong\pi(\dot\Psi)$ iff some $g$ conjugates the tori and the products of the characters restricted to $G^0$.
nodes.label: HMCor

nodes.name: Low-depth twisting character xi
nodes.statement: Let $\xi$ be a character of $T$ of depth strictly less than $r_0$.

nodes.name: Proof that Psi_xi is a datum
nodes.statement: The $G^1$-genericity of the character $\phi_0$ of $G^0$ of depth $r_0$ depends only on $\mathrm{Res}_{G^0_{x,r_0}}\phi$. Since $\xi\phi_0$ and $\phi_0$ coincide on $G^0_{x,r_0}$, we conclude that $\xi\phi_0$ is also a $G^1$-generic character of $G^0$ of depth $r_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Genericity depends only on the restriction to $G^0_{x,r_0}$, where $\xi\phi_0$ and $\phi_0$ agree.

nodes.name: Twisted datum Psi_xi
nodes.statement: Thus $$ \Psi_\xi = (\vec{G}, (\xi\phi_0, \phi_1,\ldots, \phi_{d-1})) $$ is another toral supercuspidal datum.
conclusions: $$ \Psi_\xi = (\vec{G}, (\xi\phi_0, \phi_1,\ldots, \phi_{d-1})) $$ is another toral supercuspidal datum
nodes.statement_short: Twisting $\phi_0$ by a character $\xi$ of depth $<r_0$ gives another toral supercuspidal datum $\Psi_\xi$.

nodes.name: Twisting kappa by an inflated character
nodes.statement: The character $\xi$ inflates to a character $\overline{\xi}$ of $\mathsf{K}$ such that $$ \kappa(\Psi_\xi) = \overline{\xi}\;\kappa(\Psi). $$
conclusions: The character $\xi$ inflates to a character $\overline{\xi}$ of $\mathsf{K}$ such that $$ \kappa(\Psi_\xi) = \overline{\xi}\;\kappa(\Psi). $$
nodes.statement_short: $\kappa(\Psi_\xi)=\overline{\xi}\,\kappa(\Psi)$ for the inflation $\overline{\xi}$ of $\xi$ to $\mathsf{K}$.
nodes.label: L:Murn

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement: Since $\xi$ is a character of $T=G^0=\mathsf{K}^0$ of depth less than $r_0$, it is trivial on $G^0_{x,r_0}$. Since $\mathsf{K}^1=\mathsf{K}^0\mathsf{J}^1$ and $\mathsf{K}^0\cap \mathsf{J}^1 = G^0_{x,r_0}$, $\xi$ may be uniquely inflated to a character $\xi' = \inf_{\mathsf{K}^0}^{\mathsf{K}^1}\xi$ of $\mathsf{K}^1$ that is trivial on $\mathsf{J}^1$. In particular, for any $k\in \mathsf{K}^0$, $j\in \mathsf{J}^{1}$, we have $\xi'(kj)=\xi(k)$. Since $\phi_0$ and $\xi\phi_0$ coincide on $G^0_{x,r_0}$, we may denote the extension to $\mathsf{J}^1_+$ of their common restriction by $\hat\phi_0$ and, if applicable, the corresponding Heisenberg-Weil representation of $\mathsf{K}^0 \ltimes \mathsf{J}^1$ by $\omega$. Using now \eqref{E:phi'1} and \eqref{E:phi'2}, as applicable, to construct $(\xi\phi_0)'$ and $\phi_0'$, we deduce that in both cases $(\xi\phi_0)' = \xi' \phi_0'$. Set $\overline{\xi} = \inf_{\mathsf{K}^1}^{\mathsf{K}}\xi'$; then $\inf_{\mathsf{K}^1}^{\mathsf{K}}\xi'\phi_0' = \overline{\xi}\kappa_0$. Since for $i>0$, $\kappa_i$ depends only on the character $\phi_i$, we conclude that $\overline{\xi}$ factors out of the tensor product to yield $ \kappa(\Psi_\xi) = \overline{\xi}\kappa(\Psi), $ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Inflate $\xi$ trivially across $\mathsf{J}^1$ and check through the construction of $\phi_0'$ that the twist factors out of $\kappa$.

nodes.name: Inequivalence of low-depth twists
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be a toral supercuspidal datum and suppose $\xi$ is a character of $T=G^0$ of depth less than that of $\phi_0$. If $\Psi_\xi = (\vec{G}, (\xi\phi_0, \phi_1,\ldots,\phi_{d-1}))$, then $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $G$ and it is equivalent to $\pi(\Psi)$ if and only if $\xi$ is trivial.
assumptions: Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be a toral supercuspidal datum and suppose $\xi$ is a character of $T=G^0$ of depth less than that of $\phi_0$.
If $\Psi_\xi = (\vec{G}, (\xi\phi_0, \phi_1,\ldots,\phi_{d-1}))$
conclusions: $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $G$ and it is equivalent to $\pi(\Psi)$ if and only if $\xi$ is trivial.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi(\Psi_\xi)\cong\pi(\Psi)$ iff the low-depth twist $\xi$ is trivial.
nodes.label: P:inequiv

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.3
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\pi(\Psi) \cong \pi(\Psi_\xi)$. In the setting of Lemma~\ref{HMCor}, this means there is some $g \in N_G(T)$ such that $\mathrm{Res}_{T}(\phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})=\mathrm{Res}_{T}{}^g(\xi \phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})$. Then ${}^g(\xi\phi_0){}^g\phi_1\cdots {}^g \phi_{d-1}$ is a refactorization of $\phi_0\cdots \phi_{d-1}$, in the sense of \cite[Definition 5.3]{Murnaghan2011}, and so by \cite[Proposition 5.4]{Murnaghan2011}, for each $i>0$, $\prod_{j=i}^d \phi_j$ and $\prod_{j=i}^d {}^g\phi_j$ coincide on $G^i_{x,r_{i-1}+}$. The genericity of the characters $\phi_j$ recursively implies, as in the proof of \cite[Proposition 5.6]{Murnaghan2011}, that $g\in G^1$, and so ${}^g\phi_i=\phi_i$ for all $i\geq 1$. Therefore our equality reduces to $\mathrm{Res}_{T_{r_0}} \phi_0 = \mathrm{Res}_{T_{r_0}} {}^g(\xi\phi_0) = \mathrm{Res}_{T_{r_0}} {}^g\phi_0$, whence $g\in T$ by genericity. Returning to the first equality we conclude that $\xi$ is the trivial character of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Hakim-Murnaghan criterion; Murnaghan's refactorization results and genericity force $g\in T$, so $\xi$ is trivial.

nodes.name: Bruhat-Tits description of pointwise stabilizers
nodes.statement: Given a subset $\Omega \subseteq {\mathcal{A}}$, the subgroup of $G$ that fixes $\Omega$ pointwise is generated by $Z_{\mathrm{b}}$ (the maximal bounded subgroup of the maximal torus $Z$) and those $G_\psi$ satisfying $\psi(z) \geq 0$ for each $z\in \Omega$ \cite[\S 6.4]{BruhatTits1972}.
assumptions: Given a subset $\Omega \subseteq {\mathcal{A}}$
conclusions: the subgroup of $G$ that fixes $\Omega$ pointwise is generated by $Z_{\mathrm{b}}$ (the maximal bounded subgroup of the maximal torus $Z$) and those $G_\psi$ satisfying $\psi(z) \geq 0$ for each $z\in \Omega$
nodes.statement_short: The pointwise stabilizer of $\Omega\subseteq\mathcal{A}$ is generated by $Z_b$ and the $G_\psi$ with $\psi\ge0$ on $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Geodesic [x,y]
nodes.statement: For $x,y\in {\mathcal{A}}$ we write $[x,y]$ for the geodesic from $x$ to $y$; then $G_{[x,y]} = G_x\cap G_y$.

nodes.name: Root values alpha(z-x)
nodes.statement: Given two points $x,z\in {\mathcal{A}}$, we identify $z-x$ with a vector in $X_*(S)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{R}$, and then for each $\alpha \in \Phi$, $\alpha(z-x)$ is a well-defined real number.

nodes.name: Moy-Prasad subgroups fix neighbourhoods
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal{A}}={\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{S},F)$ be an apartment in $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{G},F)$ containing $x$ and let $\Phi=\Phi(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{S})$ be the corresponding root system. Let $s \geq 0$ and define $$ \Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)=\{ z \in {\mathcal{A}} \mid \forall \alpha \in \Phi, \alpha(z-x) \leq s\}. $$ Then $G_{x,s} \subseteq G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)} = G_{\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}}$, where $\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}$ denotes the simplicial closure of $\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)$ in ${\mathcal{A}}$.
assumptions: Let ${\mathcal{A}}={\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{S},F)$ be an apartment in $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{G},F)$ containing $x$ and let $\Phi=\Phi(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{S})$ be the corresponding root system.
Let $s \geq 0$
conclusions: Then $G_{x,s} \subseteq G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)} = G_{\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}}$
nodes.statement_short: $G_{x,s}$ fixes pointwise $\Omega_{\mathcal{A}}(x,s)=\{z:\alpha(z-x)\le s\ \forall\alpha\}$ and its simplicial closure.
nodes.label: L:stabilizers

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement: That $G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)} = G_{\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}}$ follows from \cite[2.4.13]{BruhatTits1972}, since $G$ is semisimple and simply connected. Let $z\in \Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)$. For each affine root $\psi$ such that $\psi(x)\geq s$, let $\alpha$ denote its gradient. Then $\psi(x)-\psi(z) = \alpha(x-z) \leq s$ so $\psi(z) \geq \psi(x)-s \geq 0$. Thus for all affine roots $\psi$, if $G_\psi \subset G_{x,s}$ then $G_\psi \subset G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}$. Since also $Z_s \subseteq Z_{\mathrm{b}}$, we conclude $G_{x,s}\subseteq G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bruhat-Tits gives the closure statement; each affine root subgroup in $G_{x,s}$ has $\psi\ge0$ on $\Omega_{\mathcal{A}}(x,s)$.

nodes.name: Neighbourhood Omega(x,s)
nodes.statement: More generally, we may define $$ \Omega(x,s) = \bigcup_{{\mathcal{A}} \ni x} \Omega_{\mathcal{A}}(x,s) $$ which is the union over all apartments of $\mathcal{B}(G)$ containing $x$.

nodes.name: Simplicial closure of Omega(x,s)
nodes.statement: Let $\overline{\Omega(x,s)}$ denote its simplicial closure.

nodes.name: Simplicial radius
nodes.statement: Let $\Omega \subset \mathcal{B}(G)$ be a bounded convex set and suppose $x\in \Omega$. For each apartment ${\mathcal{A}} = {\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{S},F)$ containing $x$ define $$ r(\Omega, {\mathcal{A}}, x) = \sup\{\alpha(z-x) \mid z \in \Omega\cap{\mathcal{A}}, \alpha \in \Phi(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{S})\}. $$ Then the \emph{simplicial radius} of $\Omega$ with respect to $x$ is defined to be $$ c(\Omega,x) = \sup\{r(\Omega, {\mathcal{A}}, x) \mid x \in {\mathcal{A}}\}. $$
nodes.statement_short: $c(\Omega,x)$ is the sup over apartments through $x$ of $\sup\alpha(z-x)$ for $z\in\Omega$ and roots $\alpha$.
nodes.label: Def:simplicialradius

nodes.name: Simplicial radius of Omega(x,s) and of the closure of {x}
nodes.statement: As one motivating example, note that the simplicial radius of $\Omega(x,s)$ with respect to $x$ is $c(\Omega(x,s),x)=s$. For another, letting $\overline{\{x\}}$ denote the simplicial closure of $\{x\}$ in $\mathcal{B}(G)$, we have $c(\overline{\{x\}},x)<1$ since $\overline{\{x\}}$ is constrained between adjacent affine root hyperplanes in any apartment containing $x$. Note that in each of these examples we have the equality $c(\Omega,x)=r(\Omega,{\mathcal{A}},x)$ for each apartment ${\mathcal{A}}$ containing $x$.
nodes.statement_short: $c(\Omega(x,s),x)=s$ and $c(\overline{\{x\}},x)<1$.

nodes.name: Simplicial radius c_x at optimal points
nodes.statement: One can be slightly more precise about $c(\overline{\{x\}},x)$ when $x$ arises as the point identified with $\mathcal{B}(T)$ from a datum $\Psi$. In this case, $x$ is an \emph{optimal point} of $\mathcal{B}(G)$, in the sense of \cite[\S6.1]{MoyPrasad1994}, whence the family of such values $c_x=c(\overline{\{x\}}, x)$ could be computed for any $G$. For example, if $G=\mathrm{SL}_n(F)$, then the optimal points are among the barycentres of the facets, whence if $x$ lies in a $k$-dimensional facet $\mathcal{F}$ then $c_x= 1-\frac1k$.
nodes.statement_short: $x$ is an optimal point, so $c_x$ is computable; for $\mathrm{SL}_n$ with $x$ in a $k$-dimensional facet, $c_x=1-1/k$.

nodes.name: Mackey component
nodes.statement: Mackey theory gives a decomposition $$ \mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi \cong \bigoplus_{g \in G_y\backslash G/\mathsf{K}}\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y\cap {}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa, $$ where each \emph{Mackey component} $\tau(g):=\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y\cap {}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa$ is a finite-dimensional representation of $G_y$.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types
nodes.statement_short: Mackey: $\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi=\bigoplus_g\tau(g)$ with $\tau(g)=\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y\cap{}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y}{}^g\kappa$.

nodes.name: Parametrization of Mackey components by vertices
nodes.statement: Note that since $G_y=N_G(G_y)$, the Mackey components are parametrized by a subset of the $G$-orbit of the vertex $y$ in $\mathcal{B}(G)$.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: Mackey components on stabilizers containing K are types
nodes.statement: If $\mathsf{K} \subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$ then $(G_y,\tau(g))$ is a type for $\pi$.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types
assumptions: If $\mathsf{K} \subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$
conclusions: $(G_y,\tau(g))$ is a type for $\pi$.
nodes.label: P:type

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.1
nodes.statement: Consider instead the twisted Mackey component $$ {}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g) = {}^{g^{-1}}(\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y\cap {}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa) \cong \mathrm{Ind}_{G_{g^{-1}y}\cap \mathsf{K}}^{G_{g^{-1}y}} \kappa $$ which is a representation of $G_{g^{-1}y}$. If $\mathsf{K}\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$, then ${}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g) \cong \mathrm{Ind}_{\mathsf{K}}^{G_{g^{-1}y}}\kappa$. By the transitivity of compact induction, $\textrm{c-}\mathrm{Ind}_{G_{g^{-1}y}}^G\tau' = \pi$, whence by Frobenius reciprocity $(G_{g^{-1}y},{}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g))$ is a type for $\pi$, and the result follows.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types
nodes.statement_short: Conjugate the Mackey component to $\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathsf{K}}^{G_{g^{-1}y}}\kappa$ and use transitivity of induction and Frobenius reciprocity.

nodes.name: Mackey components killed by low-depth twists contain no types
nodes.statement: Given $y, \Psi, g$ as above, suppose that there exists a nontrivial character $\xi$ of $T$ of depth less than $r_0$ such that its inflation $\overline{\xi}$ to $\mathsf{K}$ is trivial on $\mathsf{K} \cap G_{g^{-1}y}$. Then no irreducible subrepresentation of the Mackey component $$ \mathrm{Ind}_{G_y \cap {}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa(\Psi) $$ is a type.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types
assumptions: Given $y, \Psi, g$ as above, suppose that there exists a nontrivial character $\xi$ of $T$ of depth less than $r_0$ such that its inflation $\overline{\xi}$ to $\mathsf{K}$ is trivial on $\mathsf{K} \cap G_{g^{-1}y}$.
conclusions: Then no irreducible subrepresentation of the Mackey component $$ \mathrm{Ind}_{G_y \cap {}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa(\Psi) $$ is a type.
nodes.statement_short: If a nontrivial low-depth character's inflation is trivial on $\mathsf{K}\cap G_{g^{-1}y}$, the Mackey component $\tau(g)$ contains no type.
nodes.label: T:inequiv

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.2
nodes.statement: The twisted Mackey component ${}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g)$ depends only $\mathrm{Res}_{G_{g^{-1}y}\cap \mathsf{K}}\kappa(\Psi)$. By Lemma~\ref{L:Murn}, $\kappa(\Psi_\xi)=\overline{\xi}\kappa(\Psi)$; by hypothesis $\mathrm{Res}_{G_{g^{-1}y}\cap\mathsf{K}}\overline{\xi}$ is trivial. Thus $\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y \cap {}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa(\Psi)$ is a common component of both $\pi(\Psi)$ and $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$. By Proposition~\ref{P:inequiv}, $\pi(\Psi)\not\cong\pi(\Psi_\xi)$. Since these are inequivalent irreducible supercuspidal representations, they have distinct inertial support, and thus no irreducible representation of $G_y$ occurring in $\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y \cap {}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa(\Psi)$ can be a type.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types
nodes.statement_short: The component is shared by $\pi(\Psi)$ and the inequivalent $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$, so it cannot contain a type.

nodes.name: Obvious types
nodes.statement: Suppose $y$ is a vertex of the facet containing $x$. Then $(G_y,\tau(1))$ is a type.
assumptions: Suppose $y$ is a vertex of the facet containing $x$.
conclusions: Then $(G_y,\tau(1))$ is a type.
nodes.label: L:obvious

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7.1
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the facet containing $x$. We have $\mathsf{K}\subseteq G_x$. Since $y \in \overline{\mathcal{F}}$ by hypothesis, $G_x \subseteq G_y$. This implies that $\mathsf{K}\subseteq G_y$, whence the first statement by Proposition~\ref{P:type}.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathsf{K}\subseteq G_x\subseteq G_y$, then apply Proposition 6.1.

nodes.name: Geodesic criterion for absence of types
nodes.statement: Let $g \in G$. Suppose that there exists $z\in [x,g^{-1}y]\cap \overline{\Omega(x,s_0)}$ such that $T \not\subseteq G_z$. Then no irreducible subrepresentation of $\tau(g)$ is a type.
assumptions: Let $g \in G$.
Suppose that there exists $z\in [x,g^{-1}y]\cap \overline{\Omega(x,s_0)}$ such that $T \not\subseteq G_z$.
conclusions: Then no irreducible subrepresentation of $\tau(g)$ is a type.
nodes.statement_short: If the geodesic $[x,g^{-1}y]$ meets $\overline{\Omega(x,s_0)}$ at a point not fixed by $T$, then $\tau(g)$ contains no type.
nodes.label: P:line

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.2
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal{A}}$ be an apartment of $\mathcal{B}(G)$ containing $x$ and $g^{-1}y$; then ${\mathcal{A}}$ contains the geodesic $[x,g^{-1}y]$. Let $z\in [x,g^{-1}y]\cap \overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s_0)}$ as in the proposition. Since $z$ is on the line $[x,g^{-1}y]$, whose pointwise stabilizer is $G_x\cap G_{g^{-1}y}$, we have that $G_x\cap G_{g^{-1}y} \subseteq G_z$. At the same time, Lemma~\ref{L:stabilizers} implies that $G_{x,s_0}\subseteq G_{\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s_0)}}\subseteq G_z$. Thus $$ \mathsf{K} \cap G_{g^{-1}y} \subseteq TG_{x,s_0} \cap G_x \cap G_{g^{-1}y} \subseteq TG_{x,s_0}\cap G_z = (T\cap G_z)G_{x,s_0}. $$ Noting that $T_{s_0} \subseteq T\cap G_z$, we deduce that any character of $T$ that is trivial on $T\cap G_z$ has depth strictly less than $s_0$. By hypothesis $T\cap G_z \subsetneq T$; so let $\xi$ be a nontrivial character of $T$ that is trivial on $T\cap G_z$. Since its depth is less than $s_0$, its inflation $\overline{\xi}$ is trivial on $(T\cap G_z)G_{x,s_0}$. We deduce that $\xi$ satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{T:inequiv}, whence the result.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\mathsf{K}\cap G_{g^{-1}y}\subseteq(T\cap G_z)G_{x,s_0}$ via Lemma 5.1, then build a nontrivial character trivial on $T\cap G_z$ and apply Theorem 6.2.

nodes.name: Fixed point set B^T
nodes.statement: Let $$ \mathcal{B}^T = \{z\in \mathcal{B}(G) \mid T\subseteq G_z\} $$ be the set of fixed points of $T$ acting on $\mathcal{B}(G)$.

nodes.name: B^T is compact convex
nodes.statement: This is a convex subset of $\mathcal{B}(G)$ containing $x$, and it is compact since $T$ is an anisotropic maximal torus.
conclusions: This is a convex subset of $\mathcal{B}(G)$ containing $x$, and it is compact

nodes.name: Simplicial radius c_T
nodes.statement: Let $c_T$ denote the simplicial radius of $\mathcal{B}^T$ with respect to $x$, as per Definition~\ref{Def:simplicialradius}.

nodes.name: Sufficient condition s_0 > c_T for Proposition 7.2
nodes.statement: Now let ${\mathcal{A}}$ be an apartment containing $x$. The hypothesis of Proposition~\ref{P:line} will be satisfied for all $g^{-1}y\in {\mathcal{A}}$ if ${\mathcal{A}}^T={\mathcal{A}} \cap \mathcal{B}^T$ is contained in the interior of the simplicial closure $\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s_0)}$ of $\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s_0)$. In particular this holds if $s_0> c_T \geq r(\mathcal{B}^T,{\mathcal{A}},x)$.
conclusions: The hypothesis of Proposition~\ref{P:line} will be satisfied for all $g^{-1}y\in {\mathcal{A}}$ if ${\mathcal{A}}^T={\mathcal{A}} \cap \mathcal{B}^T$ is contained in the interior of the simplicial closure $\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s_0)}$ of $\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s_0)$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 7.2 applies on an apartment once $\mathcal{A}^T$ lies inside $\overline{\Omega_{\mathcal{A}}(x,s_0)}$, e.g. when $s_0>c_T$.

nodes.name: Unicity of types for toral supercuspidal representations
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a tamely ramified anisotropic maximal torus of $G$ and let $s_0>c_T$. Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be any toral supercuspidal datum such that $G^0=T$ and such that the depth of $\phi_0$ is at least $2s_0$. Then $\pi(\Psi)$ satisfies the conjecture of unicity of types relative to any maximal compact open subgroup of $G$. If moreover $\mathcal{B}^T$ is the closure of a single facet of $\mathcal{B}(G)$ then $\pi(\Psi)$ has the property of strong unicity.
assumptions: Let $T$ be a tamely ramified  anisotropic maximal torus of $G$ and let $s_0>c_T$.
Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be any toral supercuspidal datum such that $G^0=T$ and such that the depth of $\phi_0$ is at least $2s_0$.
If moreover $\mathcal{B}^T$ is the closure of a single facet of $\mathcal{B}(G)$
conclusions: Then $\pi(\Psi)$ satisfies the conjecture of unicity of types relative to any maximal compact open subgroup of $G$.
then $\pi(\Psi)$ has the property of strong unicity.
nodes.statement_short: If depth$(\phi_0)\ge 2s_0>2c_T$, $\pi(\Psi)$ satisfies unicity of types; strong unicity if $\mathcal{B}^T$ is a single facet closure.
nodes.label: T:unicity

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.3
nodes.statement: Let $g\in G_y\backslash G / \mathsf{K}$. Suppose first that $g^{-1}y \in \mathcal{B}^T$, so that $T\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$. Since $s_0>c_T$, we have $g^{-1}y \in \Omega(x,s_0)$ so $G_{x,s_0}\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$ as well. Thus $\mathsf{K} \subseteq TG_{x,s_0} \subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$ and by the same argument as Lemma~\ref{L:obvious}, we conclude that $(G_{y},\tau(g))$ is a type for $\pi$. Now suppose that $g^{-1}y \notin \mathcal{B}^T$, so that $T \not\subset G_{g^{-1}y}$. Since $s_0>c_T$, $\Omega(x,s_0)$ contains an open neighbourhood of $\mathcal{B}^T$, so the line $[x,g^{-1}y]$ must meet $\Omega(x,s_0) \setminus \mathcal{B}^T$ in at least one point $z$. Using now Proposition~\ref{P:line}, we conclude that the corresponding Mackey component contains no types for $\pi(\Psi)$. Finally, we note that if $\mathcal{B}^T = \overline{\mathcal{F}}$ for a facet $\mathcal{F}\subset\mathcal{B}(G)$, then since $G$ is semisimple simply connected, each orbit of a vertex $y$ in $\mathcal{B}(G)$ meets $\mathcal{B}^T$ at most once. By the above arguments, this implies strong unicity.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on whether $g^{-1}y\in\mathcal{B}^T$: if so $\tau(g)$ is a type as in Lemma 7.1; if not the geodesic meets $\Omega(x,s_0)\setminus\mathcal{B}^T$ and Proposition 7.2 applies.

If $\mathcal{B}^T$ contains two distinct but $G$-conjugate vertices $y$ and $y'$ of alcoves whose closure contain $x$, then for any toral supercuspidal datum $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ such that $G^0=T$, the strong unicity property fails to hold for $\pi(\Psi)$, that is, there exist at least two nonisomorphic types in $\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi(\Psi)$.

conclusions: the strong unicity property fails to hold for $\pi(\Psi)$, that is, there exist at least two nonisomorphic types in $\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi(\Psi)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.1
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \mathcal{B}(T) \subseteq \mathcal{B}(G)$ and set $\pi=\pi(\Psi)$. Let $y\neq y'$ be $G$-conjugate vertices of two distinct alcoves $\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{C}'$ of $\mathcal{B}(G)$ such that $x \in \overline{\mathcal{C}}\cap \overline{\mathcal{C}'}$. Then for any $s_0>0$, we have that $y,y' \in \overline{\Omega(x,s_0)}$. Let $g \in G$ be such that $y'=g^{-1}y$. If both $y$ and $g^{-1}y$ lie in $\mathcal{B}^T$, then by the proof of Theorem~\ref{T:unicity}, we conclude that both $(G_y,\tau(1))$ and $(G_{y},\tau(g))$ are types for $\pi$ occurring in $\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi$. Note that although these types are induced from the $G$-conjugate types $(\mathsf{K},\kappa)$ and $({}^g\mathsf{K},{}^g\kappa)$, they are not themselves $G$-conjugate since $g\notin N_G(G_y)=G_y$. Neither are these types isomorphic, since $\pi \cong \textrm{c-}\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y}^G\tau(1)$ implies $$ \mathbb{C}\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{G}(\pi,\pi) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_{G_y}(\tau(1),\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi) $$ by Frobenius reciprocity.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity
nodes.statement_short: Both $\tau(1)$ and $\tau(g)$ with $y'=g^{-1}y$ are types on $G_y$; they are non-conjugate since $g\notin G_y$ and non-isomorphic by Frobenius reciprocity.

nodes.name: Fixed points and exactly two types in the Sp_4 example
nodes.statement: In the setting of the preceding example, we can conclude slightly more. First note that if $z\in {\mathcal{A}}$ and $T\subseteq G_z$, then for each positive long root $\alpha$, we must have $0\leq \alpha(z)\leq 1$. It follows that ${\mathcal{A}}^T = \overline{\mathcal{C}}\cup\overline{w\mathcal{C}}$, as indicated in Figure~\ref{Fig:1}. We claim that in fact $\mathcal{B}^T={\mathcal{A}}^T$. Since $G_x\cap G_y=G_\mathcal{C}$, the orbit of $y$ is parametrized by the set $G_x/G_\mathcal{C} \simeq \mathrm{GL}_2({\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}})/\mathcal{I}$, where $\mathcal{I}$ denotes its Iwahori subgroup. A set of representatives is $$ \left\{\overline{a} = \bmat{1&a&&\\0&1&& \\ && 1&0\\&&-a&1}, w= \bmat{0&1&&\\-1&0&&\\&&0&1\\&&-1&0} \;\;\middle| \;\;a \in {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}/\mathfrak{p} \right\}. $$ One can verify directly that for each $a \in {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}^\times$, ${}^{\overline{a}} T\not\subseteq G_y$. Thus since the fixed point set $\mathcal{B}^T$ is closed and convex but contains no vertices of chambers adjacent to $x$ outside of ${\mathcal{A}}$, we conclude that $\mathcal{B}^T=\overline{\mathcal{C}}\cup \overline{w\mathcal{C}}={\mathcal{A}}^T$, which is contained entirely in the standard apartment. Therefore we can compute the simplicial radius of $\mathcal{B}^T$ with respect to $x$, yielding $c_T=\frac12$. We had see that $\tau(1)$ and $\tau(w)$ gave types. For $a\in {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}^\times$, since the choice $z=\overline{a}^{-1}y$ satisfies the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{P:line} for any $s_0>0$, we deduce that the corresponding Mackey components $\tau(\overline{a})$ do not contain types. For the remaining Mackey components, $g^{-1}y$ is not in the closure of an alcove adjacent to $x$, and Theorem~\ref{T:unicity} implies that if $s_0>c_T=\frac12$, any corresponding toral supercuspidal representation contains exactly the two types on $G_y$ identified above.

nodes.statement_short: In the $\mathrm{Sp}_4$ example $\mathcal{B}^T=\overline{\mathcal{C}}\cup\overline{w\mathcal{C}}$, $c_T=1/2$, and for $s_0>1/2$ there are exactly two types on $G_y$.
nodes.label: R:ex

nodes.name: Exponentially many types for Sp_2n
nodes.statement: Let $n\geq 2$ and consider the subgroup $G' \cong \mathrm{SL}_2(F)^n$ of $G=\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}(F)$ generated by the root subgroups corresponding to long roots. To allow us to be explicit, let the roots of $\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}$ with respect to the diagonal torus $\mathbf{S}$ be the set $\Phi=\{\varepsilon_i\pm \varepsilon_j, \pm2\varepsilon_i \mid 1\leq i \neq j \leq n\}$, with simple system $\Delta=\{\varepsilon_i-\varepsilon_{i+1}, 2\varepsilon_n\mid 1\leq i < n\}$. With respect to the basis $\{e_1,\ldots, e_n\}$ of $X_*(\mathbf{S})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{R}$ (whose affine space is ${\mathcal{A}}$), dual to $\{\varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_n\}$, the vertices of the fundamental alcove $\mathcal{C}$ are $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^i \frac12e_j$, for $0\leq i \leq n$. Let $W=W_{\mathbf{G}}$ denote the Weyl group of $\mathbf{G}$ relative to $\mathbf{S}$. In $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$, there are two conjugacy classes of unramified anisotropic tori, attached to the distinct conjugacy classes of vertices in $\mathcal{B}(\mathrm{SL}_2,F)$. There are between 2 and 4 conjugacy classes of ramified anisotropic tori, attached to the midpoint of facets; see \cite{Nevins2013}, for example. With respect to the coordinates above, the roots of each $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ subgroup are $\pm 2\varepsilon_i$, and thus up to conjugacy we can arrange that the vertices have $e_i$-coordinates in $\{0,\frac12\}$, whereas the midpoints have $e_i$-coordinate $\frac14$. Let each of $T_1,\ldots, T_n$ represent an anisotropic torus of $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$, ordered so that: for $1\leq i\leq m$, $T_i$ is unramified and attached to $\frac12$; for $m+1\leq i \leq m+\ell$, $T_i$ is ramified and attached to $\frac14$; and for $i>m+\ell$, $T_i$ is again unramified, but attached to $0$. Then $T=T_1\times \cdots \times T_n$ embeds as an anisotropic maximal torus of $G$, and $\{x\} = \mathcal{B}(T)\subseteq \mathcal{B}(G)$ has coordinates $$ x = \sum_{j=1}^m \frac12e_j + \sum_{j=m+1}^{m+\ell} \frac14e_j. $$ This is the midpoint of the $1$-dimensional facet $\mathcal{F}$ whose closure is the geodesic $[v_m, v_{m+\ell}]$. Let $\Omega = \{\sum_{j=1}^m \frac12e_j + \sum_{j=m+1}^{m+\ell} a_je_j \mid 0\leq a_j \leq \frac12\}$; then $\mathcal{F} \subseteq \Omega$ and one can verify directly that $\Omega = \{z \in {\mathcal{A}} \mid T\subseteq G_z\}={\mathcal{A}}^T$ using the argument of Remark~\ref{R:ex}. Note that since every maximal facet of $\Omega$ has $x$ in its closure, $\Omega \subseteq \overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}$ for any $s>0$. Note that $\overline{\mathcal{F}} \neq \Omega$ if and only if $\ell>1$. In this case, let $W^\Omega = \{ w\in W\mid w\Omega \subseteq \Omega\}$ and let $W_{\Omega} = \{ w\in W\mid \forall z\in \Omega, wz=z \}$. The elements of $W(T) := W^\Omega/W_{\Omega}$ permute the vertices of $\Omega$. Let $\mathbf{G}' = \mathrm{Sp}_{2m}\times \mathrm{SL}_2^\ell \times \mathrm{Sp}_{2n-2m-2\ell}\subseteq \mathbf{G}$; then we can identify $W(T)$ with $W_\mathbf{G}/W_{\mathbf{G}'}$. The vertices of $\Omega\cap \mathcal{C}$ are $v_{m}, \ldots, v_{m+\ell}$. The vertices $v_m$ and $v_{m+\ell}$ are fixed by each element of $W(T)$, but the orbit of $y=v_{m+t}$ under $W(T)$, for $0<t<\ell$, contains $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} \ell\\ t\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ distinct vertices of $\Omega$. Let $\Psi$ be any toral supercuspidal datum such that $G^0=T$, and $\pi=\pi(\Psi)$. By the argument of the proof of Lemma~\ref{L:strongunicityfails}, for each vertex $y=v_{m+t}$ with $0<t<\ell$, $\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi$ contains $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} \ell\\ t\end{smallmatrix}\right)>1$ inequivalent types.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity
nodes.statement_short: Products of $\mathrm{SL}_2$ tori in $\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}$ give $\binom{\ell}{t}>1$ inequivalent types on $G_{v_{m+t}}$.
nodes.label: Ex:2

nodes.name: Broader classes of tori
nodes.statement: The quadratic tori of Examples~\ref{Ex:1} and \ref{Ex:2} are the smallest of a broad class of tori to which the preceding arguments apply. For example, using L.~Morris's classification of anisotropic maximal principal tori of $\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}(F)$ in \cite{Morris1991} one can explicitly construct products of tori of arbitrary rank, obtaining analogous results. Similar constructive arguments may be made for groups of type $B_n$ and $D_n$.

nodes.name: Hurst: Coxeter tori and fixed points
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses that $\mathbf{G}$ is simple, connected and split over $F$ (but not of type $E_7$ or $E_8$), that $T$ splits over a purely tamely ramified cyclic Galois extension, and some mild assumptions on $F$, Hurst proves that $\mathcal{B}^{T_{0+}} = \overline{\{x\}}$ if and only if $T$ is a Coxeter torus (in which case $x$ lies in an alcove) \cite[Satz 13.14]{Hurstthesis}.

assumptions: Under the hypotheses that $\mathbf{G}$ is simple, connected and split over $F$ (but not of type $E_7$ or $E_8$), that $T$ splits over a purely tamely ramified cyclic Galois extension, and some mild assumptions on $F$

nodes.statement: Then it follows that $\mathcal{B}^{T_{0+}}$ contains the closure of the $G_x$-orbit of this alcove in $\mathcal{B}(G)$, since $T_{0+}\subseteq G_{x,0+} \subseteq G_{\mathcal{C}}$ for all alcoves $\mathcal{C}$ adjacent to $x$.

conclusions: $\mathcal{B}^{T_{0+}}$ contains the closure of the $G_x$-orbit of this alcove in $\mathcal{B}(G)$

nodes.name: Inflate xi to K^1
nodes.statement: Since $\xi$ is a character of $T=G^0=\mathsf{K}^0$ of depth less than $r_0$, it is trivial on $G^0_{x,r_0}$. Since $\mathsf{K}^1=\mathsf{K}^0\mathsf{J}^1$ and $\mathsf{K}^0\cap \mathsf{J}^1 = G^0_{x,r_0}$, $\xi$ may be uniquely inflated to a character $\xi' = \inf_{\mathsf{K}^0}^{\mathsf{K}^1}\xi$ of $\mathsf{K}^1$ that is trivial on $\mathsf{J}^1$. In particular, for any $k\in \mathsf{K}^0$, $j\in \mathsf{J}^{1}$, we have $\xi'(kj)=\xi(k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Inflate $\xi$ to $\xi'$ on $\mathsf{K}^1$, trivial on $\mathsf{J}^1$.

nodes.name: Compare the constructions
nodes.statement: Since $\phi_0$ and $\xi\phi_0$ coincide on $G^0_{x,r_0}$, we may denote the extension to $\mathsf{J}^1_+$ of their common restriction by $\hat\phi_0$ and, if applicable, the corresponding Heisenberg-Weil representation of $\mathsf{K}^0 \ltimes \mathsf{J}^1$ by $\omega$. Using now \eqref{E:phi'1} and \eqref{E:phi'2}, as applicable, to construct $(\xi\phi_0)'$ and $\phi_0'$, we deduce that in both cases $(\xi\phi_0)' = \xi' \phi_0'$.
nodes.statement_short: Both data share $\hat\phi_0$ and $\omega$, so $(\xi\phi_0)'=\xi'\phi_0'$.

nodes.name: Factor out of the tensor product
nodes.statement: Set $\overline{\xi} = \inf_{\mathsf{K}^1}^{\mathsf{K}}\xi'$; then $\inf_{\mathsf{K}^1}^{\mathsf{K}}\xi'\phi_0' = \overline{\xi}\kappa_0$. Since for $i>0$, $\kappa_i$ depends only on the character $\phi_i$, we conclude that $\overline{\xi}$ factors out of the tensor product to yield $ \kappa(\Psi_\xi) = \overline{\xi}\kappa(\Psi), $ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Inflate to $\mathsf{K}$; $\overline{\xi}$ factors out of $\kappa$ since other $\kappa_i$ are unchanged.

nodes.name: Apply Hakim-Murnaghan
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\pi(\Psi) \cong \pi(\Psi_\xi)$. In the setting of Lemma~\ref{HMCor}, this means there is some $g \in N_G(T)$ such that $\mathrm{Res}_{T}(\phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})=\mathrm{Res}_{T}{}^g(\xi \phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalence gives $g\in N_G(T)$ matching the character products on $T$.

nodes.name: Refactorization
nodes.statement: Then ${}^g(\xi\phi_0){}^g\phi_1\cdots {}^g \phi_{d-1}$ is a refactorization of $\phi_0\cdots \phi_{d-1}$, in the sense of \cite[Definition 5.3]{Murnaghan2011}, and so by \cite[Proposition 5.4]{Murnaghan2011}, for each $i>0$, $\prod_{j=i}^d \phi_j$ and $\prod_{j=i}^d {}^g\phi_j$ coincide on $G^i_{x,r_{i-1}+}$.
nodes.statement_short: Murnaghan's refactorization result: partial products agree on $G^i_{x,r_{i-1}+}$.

nodes.name: g lies in G^1
nodes.statement: The genericity of the characters $\phi_j$ recursively implies, as in the proof of \cite[Proposition 5.6]{Murnaghan2011}, that $g\in G^1$, and so ${}^g\phi_i=\phi_i$ for all $i\geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Genericity forces $g\in G^1$, so $g$ fixes $\phi_i$, $i\ge1$.

nodes.name: g lies in T, so xi is trivial
nodes.statement: Therefore our equality reduces to $\mathrm{Res}_{T_{r_0}} \phi_0 = \mathrm{Res}_{T_{r_0}} {}^g(\xi\phi_0) = \mathrm{Res}_{T_{r_0}} {}^g\phi_0$, whence $g\in T$ by genericity. Returning to the first equality we conclude that $\xi$ is the trivial character of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $\phi_0$ on $T_{r_0}$, so $g\in T$ by genericity and $\xi$ is trivial.

nodes.name: Closure equality
nodes.statement: That $G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)} = G_{\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}}$ follows from \cite[2.4.13]{BruhatTits1972}, since $G$ is semisimple and simply connected.
nodes.statement_short: Stabilizer of $\Omega$ equals that of its closure by Bruhat-Tits.

nodes.name: Affine root subgroups fix Omega
nodes.statement: Let $z\in \Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)$. For each affine root $\psi$ such that $\psi(x)\geq s$, let $\alpha$ denote its gradient. Then $\psi(x)-\psi(z) = \alpha(x-z) \leq s$ so $\psi(z) \geq \psi(x)-s \geq 0$. Thus for all affine roots $\psi$, if $G_\psi \subset G_{x,s}$ then $G_\psi \subset G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\psi(x)\ge s$, $\psi(z)\ge\psi(x)-s\ge0$ on $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Conclude containment
nodes.statement: Since also $Z_s \subseteq Z_{\mathrm{b}}$, we conclude $G_{x,s}\subseteq G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Add $Z_s\subseteq Z_b$ to conclude $G_{x,s}\subseteq G_\Omega$.

nodes.name: Twist the Mackey component
nodes.statement: Consider instead the twisted Mackey component $$ {}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g) = {}^{g^{-1}}(\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y\cap {}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa) \cong \mathrm{Ind}_{G_{g^{-1}y}\cap \mathsf{K}}^{G_{g^{-1}y}} \kappa $$ which is a representation of $G_{g^{-1}y}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugate $\tau(g)$ by $g^{-1}$.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: Use the hypothesis
nodes.statement: If $\mathsf{K}\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$, then ${}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g) \cong \mathrm{Ind}_{\mathsf{K}}^{G_{g^{-1}y}}\kappa$.
nodes.statement_short: Under the hypothesis it is $\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathsf{K}}^{G_{g^{-1}y}}\kappa$.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: Transitivity and Frobenius reciprocity
nodes.statement: By the transitivity of compact induction, $\textrm{c-}\mathrm{Ind}_{G_{g^{-1}y}}^G\tau' = \pi$, whence by Frobenius reciprocity $(G_{g^{-1}y},{}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g))$ is a type for $\pi$, and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Transitivity of induction and Frobenius reciprocity give a type.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: Dependence on restriction
nodes.statement: The twisted Mackey component ${}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g)$ depends only $\mathrm{Res}_{G_{g^{-1}y}\cap \mathsf{K}}\kappa(\Psi)$.
nodes.statement_short: The component depends only on $\kappa$ restricted to $G_{g^{-1}y}\cap\mathsf{K}$.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: Common component
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{L:Murn}, $\kappa(\Psi_\xi)=\overline{\xi}\kappa(\Psi)$; by hypothesis $\mathrm{Res}_{G_{g^{-1}y}\cap\mathsf{K}}\overline{\xi}$ is trivial. Thus $\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y \cap {}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa(\Psi)$ is a common component of both $\pi(\Psi)$ and $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 4.2 the twist is invisible there, so the component is common to $\pi(\Psi)$ and $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: Inequivalence
nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref{P:inequiv}, $\pi(\Psi)\not\cong\pi(\Psi_\xi)$.
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 4.3 the two representations are inequivalent.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: No type
nodes.statement: Since these are inequivalent irreducible supercuspidal representations, they have distinct inertial support, and thus no irreducible representation of $G_y$ occurring in $\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y \cap {}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa(\Psi)$ can be a type.
nodes.statement_short: Distinct inertial supports, so no type occurs.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: K in G_x
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the facet containing $x$. We have $\mathsf{K}\subseteq G_x$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the facet $\mathcal{F}$; $\mathsf{K}\subseteq G_x$.

nodes.name: G_x in G_y
nodes.statement: Since $y \in \overline{\mathcal{F}}$ by hypothesis, $G_x \subseteq G_y$.
nodes.statement_short: $y\in\overline{\mathcal{F}}$ gives $G_x\subseteq G_y$.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 6.1
nodes.statement: This implies that $\mathsf{K}\subseteq G_y$, whence the first statement by Proposition~\ref{P:type}.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\mathsf{K}\subseteq G_y$ and Proposition 6.1 applies.

nodes.name: Apartment, point z and geodesic stabilizer
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal{A}}$ be an apartment of $\mathcal{B}(G)$ containing $x$ and $g^{-1}y$; then ${\mathcal{A}}$ contains the geodesic $[x,g^{-1}y]$. Let $z\in [x,g^{-1}y]\cap \overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s_0)}$ as in the proposition. Since $z$ is on the line $[x,g^{-1}y]$, whose pointwise stabilizer is $G_x\cap G_{g^{-1}y}$, we have that $G_x\cap G_{g^{-1}y} \subseteq G_z$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick an apartment and $z$ on the geodesic; then $G_x\cap G_{g^{-1}y}\subseteq G_z$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement: At the same time, Lemma~\ref{L:stabilizers} implies that $G_{x,s_0}\subseteq G_{\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s_0)}}\subseteq G_z$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.1 gives $G_{x,s_0}\subseteq G_z$.

nodes.name: Bound K cap G_{g^{-1}y} and depth
nodes.statement: Thus $$ \mathsf{K} \cap G_{g^{-1}y} \subseteq TG_{x,s_0} \cap G_x \cap G_{g^{-1}y} \subseteq TG_{x,s_0}\cap G_z = (T\cap G_z)G_{x,s_0}. $$ Noting that $T_{s_0} \subseteq T\cap G_z$, we deduce that any character of $T$ that is trivial on $T\cap G_z$ has depth strictly less than $s_0$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathsf{K}\cap G_{g^{-1}y}\subseteq (T\cap G_z)G_{x,s_0}$; characters trivial on $T\cap G_z$ have depth $<s_0$.

nodes.name: Construct xi
nodes.statement: By hypothesis $T\cap G_z \subsetneq T$; so let $\xi$ be a nontrivial character of $T$ that is trivial on $T\cap G_z$. Since its depth is less than $s_0$, its inflation $\overline{\xi}$ is trivial on $(T\cap G_z)G_{x,s_0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a nontrivial $\xi$ trivial on $T\cap G_z$; its inflation is trivial on the bound.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 6.2
nodes.statement: We deduce that $\xi$ satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{T:inequiv}, whence the result.
nodes.statement_short: $\xi$ satisfies Theorem 6.2.

nodes.name: Case g^{-1}y in B^T
nodes.statement: Let $g\in G_y\backslash G / \mathsf{K}$. Suppose first that $g^{-1}y \in \mathcal{B}^T$, so that $T\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$. Since $s_0>c_T$, we have $g^{-1}y \in \Omega(x,s_0)$ so $G_{x,s_0}\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$ as well. Thus $\mathsf{K} \subseteq TG_{x,s_0} \subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$ and by the same argument as Lemma~\ref{L:obvious}, we conclude that $(G_{y},\tau(g))$ is a type for $\pi$.
nodes.statement_short: If $g^{-1}y\in\mathcal{B}^T$, then $\mathsf{K}\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$ and $\tau(g)$ is a type.

nodes.name: Case g^{-1}y not in B^T
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $g^{-1}y \notin \mathcal{B}^T$, so that $T \not\subset G_{g^{-1}y}$. Since $s_0>c_T$, $\Omega(x,s_0)$ contains an open neighbourhood of $\mathcal{B}^T$, so the line $[x,g^{-1}y]$ must meet $\Omega(x,s_0) \setminus \mathcal{B}^T$ in at least one point $z$. Using now Proposition~\ref{P:line}, we conclude that the corresponding Mackey component contains no types for $\pi(\Psi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise the geodesic meets $\Omega(x,s_0)\setminus\mathcal{B}^T$ and Proposition 7.2 rules out types.

nodes.name: Strong unicity
nodes.statement: Finally, we note that if $\mathcal{B}^T = \overline{\mathcal{F}}$ for a facet $\mathcal{F}\subset\mathcal{B}(G)$, then since $G$ is semisimple simply connected, each orbit of a vertex $y$ in $\mathcal{B}(G)$ meets $\mathcal{B}^T$ at most once. By the above arguments, this implies strong unicity.
nodes.statement_short: If $\mathcal{B}^T$ is one facet closure, each vertex orbit meets it once: strong unicity.

nodes.name: Set up conjugate vertices
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \mathcal{B}(T) \subseteq \mathcal{B}(G)$ and set $\pi=\pi(\Psi)$. Let $y\neq y'$ be $G$-conjugate vertices of two distinct alcoves $\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{C}'$ of $\mathcal{B}(G)$ such that $x \in \overline{\mathcal{C}}\cap \overline{\mathcal{C}'}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix conjugate vertices $y\ne y'$ of alcoves adjacent to $x$.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity

nodes.name: Vertices lie in Omega
nodes.statement: Then for any $s_0>0$, we have that $y,y' \in \overline{\Omega(x,s_0)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Both vertices lie in $\overline{\Omega(x,s_0)}$ for every $s_0>0$.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity

nodes.name: Two types
nodes.statement: Let $g \in G$ be such that $y'=g^{-1}y$. If both $y$ and $g^{-1}y$ lie in $\mathcal{B}^T$, then by the proof of Theorem~\ref{T:unicity}, we conclude that both $(G_y,\tau(1))$ and $(G_{y},\tau(g))$ are types for $\pi$ occurring in $\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi$.
nodes.statement_short: By the proof of Theorem 7.3, $\tau(1)$ and $\tau(g)$ are both types.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity

nodes.name: Not conjugate
nodes.statement: Note that although these types are induced from the $G$-conjugate types $(\mathsf{K},\kappa)$ and $({}^g\mathsf{K},{}^g\kappa)$, they are not themselves $G$-conjugate since $g\notin N_G(G_y)=G_y$.
nodes.statement_short: They are not $G$-conjugate since $g\notin G_y$.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity

nodes.name: Not isomorphic
nodes.statement: Neither are these types isomorphic, since $\pi \cong \textrm{c-}\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y}^G\tau(1)$ implies $$ \mathbb{C}\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{G}(\pi,\pi) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_{G_y}(\tau(1),\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi) $$ by Frobenius reciprocity.
nodes.statement_short: Frobenius reciprocity shows $\tau(1)$ occurs once, so they are non-isomorphic.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity
